title: Euler, Heun and Runge–Kutta
subtitle: Step along the solution of dy/dx = f(x, y), using the slope — once, twice, or four times per step.

sections.title: Initial value problems
sections.body: Solve y′ = f(x, y) with y(x₀) = y₀. Numerical methods produce y at x₀, x₀ + h, x₀ + 2h, … One-step methods use only the last point. The running example is y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1, whose exact solution y = 2eˣ − x − 1 gives y(1) = 3.43656 to compare with.

choices.text: The equation and the starting value y(x₀).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Without it there are infinitely many solutions.

sections.title: Euler’s method
sections.body: yn+1 = yₙ + h·f(xₙ, yₙ): walk along the tangent. Simple, but each step has error O(h²) and the total error is O(h) — first order. Halving h halves the error: y(1) is 3.18748 with h = 0.1 and 3.3066 with h = 0.05, against the exact 3.43656.

questions.prompt: Euler’s method is first order: halving h…

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — Euler with h = 0.1
figures.note: Grey = exact, blue = Euler; the gap grows.

sections.title: Heun’s method (improved Euler)
sections.body: Predict with Euler, then average the slope at the start and at the predicted end: k₁ = f(xₙ, yₙ), k₂ = f(xₙ + h, yₙ + hk₁), yn+1 = yₙ + (h/2)(k₁ + k₂). Second-order: y(1) = 3.42816 with h = 0.1 — far closer than Euler. It is the trapezoid rule applied to the ODE.

worked.why: One Heun step from (0, 1), h = 0.1. k₁ = f(0, 1) = 1. Predictor y* = 1.1.

questions.prompt: Heun’s method improves on Euler by…

choices.text: Averaging the slopes at the start and at the predicted end of the step.

sections.title: Runge–Kutta of order 4
sections.body: The classic RK4: k₁ = f(xₙ, yₙ); k₂ = f(xₙ + h/2, yₙ + hk₁/2); k₃ = f(xₙ + h/2, yₙ + hk₂/2); k₄ = f(xₙ + h, yₙ + hk₃); yn+1 = yₙ + (h/6)(k₁ + 2k₂ + 2k₃ + k₄). Fourth-order: error ∝ h⁴ — y(1) = 3.43656 at h = 0.1, agreeing with the exact 3.43656 to five digits. Each step costs four evaluations, but it reaches a given accuracy with far larger h.

choices.text: High accuracy (order 4) without needing derivatives of f.
It uses one slope per step.

figures.note: All three against the exact curve.

problems.prompt: Solve y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1 to x = 1 with h = 0.1 using Euler and RK4. Compare with the exact 2eˣ − x − 1.

sections.title: Step size, stability and stiff equations
sections.body: Too large an h is inaccurate and, for equations like y′ = −50y, unstable (the explicit Euler method blows up when h > 2/50). Adaptive methods shrink h where the solution changes quickly (Runge–Kutta–Fehlberg compares orders 4 and 5). Stiff problems, with very different time scales, need implicit methods that stay stable at large steps.

worked.why: y₁ = y₀(1 − 50·0.05) = −1.5: the true solution decays to 0 but the numerical one grows in magnitude — instability.

questions.prompt: Euler on y′ = −50y with h = 0.05 gives…

choices.text: Growing oscillations — the step is beyond the stability limit.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: h is too large for that.

sections.title: Systems and higher-order equations
sections.body: A higher-order ODE becomes a first-order system: y″ = f(x, y, y′) → let u = y, v = y′; then u′ = v, v′ = f(x, u, v). All methods apply componentwise to the vector (u, v). This is how the notebook's physics engine advances every body: position and velocity together.

worked.why: Write y″ + y = 0 as a system.
u′ = v, v′ = −u — one Euler step from (1, 0): u₁ = 1, v₁ = −h.

questions.prompt: y″ = −y is converted to a first-order system using…

choices.text: u = y, v = y′, so u′ = v and v′ = −u.
